summary: This memo gives the BGP working group recommendation on how to advertise a default route in versions 2 and 3 of the Border Gateway Protocol. A default route is the catch-all path used when no more specific route exists. It is historic.

eli5.summary: When a router does not know where to send something, it can use a catch-all road. This paper says how one router can tell its neighbors about that catch-all road. It is historic.

questions: how to advertise a default route in bgp
subtitle: How older BGP versions advertise a fallback route

tldr.problem: Routers cannot always maintain complete routing tables, especially when the Internet was smaller and memory was scarce. They need a fallback route for destinations they do not know about explicitly.
tldr.mechanism: A BGP speaker can advertise a default route by sending an UPDATE message with the network address 0.0.0.0 and a NEXT_HOP attribute pointing to the gateway that should handle unknown traffic. Multiple defaults can be advertised with preference levels.
tldr.outcome: This recommendation applied only to BGP2 and BGP3. Starting with BGP4, default route advertisement became a built-in part of the protocol, making this recommendation obsolete.

today: RFC 1397 is Historic. BGP4, the current standard for interdomain routing specified in RFC 4271, has default route support built in. This RFC is retained for reference only, as a guide for anyone maintaining legacy BGP2 or BGP3 systems.

sections.title: Default Routes
sections.content:
A default route is a catch-all path that a router uses when it does not have an explicit routing entry for a destination address. Rather than dropping traffic destined for unknown networks, a router can forward it to a default gateway that might know what to do with it.

This is especially useful for routers that cannot maintain a complete routing table—either because the full routing table is too large to fit in memory, or to reduce the processing overhead of consulting a massive table. Instead of storing millions of routes, a router can store only the destinations it uses frequently, and forward everything else to a default gateway.
sections.eli5: If a router does not know where a package should go, it sends it to a default gateway that might know better. This saves the router from having to remember the address of every possible destination.

sections.title: Advertising a Default Route in BGP2 and BGP3
sections.content:
To advertise a default route in BGP version 2 or 3, a BGP speaker sends an UPDATE message with the network field set to 0.0.0.0, a special address that indicates a default route. The NEXT_HOP path attribute in the message specifies the IP address of the border gateway that should handle traffic destined for networks not in the router's table.

The ORIGIN attribute should be set to INCOMPLETE (value 2) because the default route is not a known path. If multiple default routes are being advertised, the INTER-AS-METRIC path attribute can express a preference order, allowing BGP speakers to favor one default gateway over another. If a previously advertised default route becomes unreachable, an UNREACHABLE message notifies neighbors.

UPDATE messages containing default routes follow the same rules as conventional route advertisements and are processed according to the receiving router's local policies.
sections.eli5: A router sends a special message saying '0.0.0.0 goes to this gateway.' Other routers read this message and know where to send traffic when they do not have a better route. If there are multiple default gateways, the router can say which one is better.

sections.title: Obsolescence in BGP4
sections.content:
RFC 1397 applies only to BGP versions 2 and 3. Starting with BGP version 4 (RFC 4271, the current standard for BGP), default route advertisement capability was built directly into the protocol design. BGP4 routers do not need to follow this recommendation because they have a standardized way of handling default routes as part of their specification.

For modern BGP deployments, default routes are handled by the standard BGP4 protocol and this RFC is Historic, retained as a reference for anyone still maintaining legacy BGP2 or BGP3 implementations.
sections.eli5: Newer versions of BGP (BGP4) learned how to advertise default routes automatically, so this paper's advice only matters if you are running an old version.
